text:
The most likely fault is the start-up pull-down Mst2 being undersized. That means the start-up circuit never turns off. This is inferred from the operating points; I did not re-simulate.

**Evidence that start-up is still on:**
- The PMOS mirror is 1:1 and equal-sized, so M3 and M4 both carry 33 nA.
- M2 carries only 27 nA. The missing ~6 nA is sunk from node g by Mst3.
- Mst3's gate (node st) sits at 0.446 V. In a working start-up, Mst2 would pull st close to 0 V once vref is up, and Mst3 would be fully off.
- Mst1's gate is tied to vss, so it is fully on and sources 1.6 µA into st. Mst2 has only Vgs = vref = 0.647 V, just above its 0.633 V threshold. Its W/L of 2/0.5 can only sink that 1.6 µA by letting st rise to about 0.45 V.
- With st there, Mst3 leaks about 18% of the core branch current from g. That leak changes with VDD, which gives the poor line regulation (0.114 V/V) and PSRR (19 dB).
- Start-up also draws about 1.6 µA × 1.8 V ≈ 2.9 µW, most of the 3.17 µW total.

**Why not M4:** M4 has the largest line-regulation sensitivity. But M3 and M4 are identical and carry equal currents, so the mirror itself is not corrupted.

**Why Mst2 over Mst1:** the fault is an imbalance between a pull-up that is too strong and a pull-down that is too weak. Their sensitivities are nearly equal and opposite (+2.54% and −2.46%), so these numbers alone can't tell which one was changed. I rank Mst2 first only on a judgement call: Mst1 at W/L = 0.5/8 looks like a deliberately weak pull-up, so a shrunk Mst2 is the more likely corruption. Changing either Mst2 or Mst1 in simulation would settle it.
